title: 430,000-Year-Old Wooden Tools Rewrite the Story of Early Human Ingenuity
summary: Deep in central Greece’s Peloponnese region, at a site called Marathousa 1, an international team of scientists has made a staggering discovery: two wooden tools that are 430,000 years old. That’s at least 40,000 years older than any previously known wooden tools, pushing back the timeline of human woodworking into the Middle Pleistocene—a crucial period for human evolution. The tools, described in the journal PNAS, were carefully shaped. One, made from alder wood, shows clear chopping and carving marks along with wear from use, suggesting it was a digging stick or bark stripper. The other, a smaller piece of willow or poplar, also bears signs of carving. “Unlike stones, wooden objects need special conditions to survive over long periods of time,” said Dr. Annemieke Milks, a leading expert in early wooden tools. The team examined the wood under microscopes, confirming the marks were made by human hands. The site, once a lakeshore, also yielded stone tools and elephant bones, indicating it was a butchering ground. But not every mark was human. A larger alder fragment had grooves made by a large carnivore, possibly a bear, highlighting the dangerous competition early humans faced. “This shows once again how exceptionally good the conditions at the Marathousa 1 site are for preservation,” said Professor Katerina Harvati, the project leader. “And the fact that large carnivores left their mark near the butchered elephant alongside human activity indicates fierce competition.” The discovery underscores the sophisticated skills of our ancestors, who weren’t just using stone but also shaping wood with precision—a craft previously thought to have emerged much later.
why_it_matters: This discovery changes the timeline of human technology, showing that our ancestors were creative problem-solvers much earlier than we thought, which reminds us that human progress is full of surprises waiting to be uncovered.

background_read: Marathousa 1 is an archaeological site in Greece’s Peloponnese region, first explored in 2013 and known for its exceptional preservation of ancient remains.
The Middle Pleistocene (about 780,000 to 126,000 years ago) was a key period for human evolution, when species like Homo heidelbergensis hunted large game and began developing more advanced tools.

Dr. Annemieke Milks is a researcher at the University of Reading specializing in early human woodworking; Professor Katerina Harvati is a leading paleoanthropologist at the University of Tübingen and the project leader at Marathousa 1.
PNAS (the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) is a top-tier American scientific journal that publishes major discoveries across many fields.
Before this find, the oldest known wooden tools were about 300,000 years old, from sites in Germany and England, so the Marathousa discovery pushes the timeline back by over 100,000 years.

perspectives.description: Archaeologists and anthropologists gain a more complete picture of early human abilities. The find proves that woodworking was a sophisticated craft far earlier than the previous oldest tools suggested, potentially reshaping museum exhibits and textbooks about the ‘Stone Age.’

Wooden artifacts are extremely rare because they usually rot away, meaning we may never know the true extent of early technology. Some scholars might question whether the marks are truly human-made or result from natural processes, though the study provides strong microscopic evidence.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral/Analytical: Co-evolution of tools and brains
perspectives.description: This find aligns with a broader pattern of incremental human innovation during the Middle Pleistocene, alongside changes in brain size and social behavior. It also illustrates how environmental preservation biases the archaeological record—what we ‘know’ depends heavily on what survives.

The discovery at Marathousa 1 could inspire archaeologists to look for wood more deliberately at other ancient lakeshore sites, using screening techniques that don’t destroy fragile organic materials. Future finds might push the origin of wooden tools back even further, possibly to a million years ago.
